title: Examination Based on Seven Virtues and Vices
description: A thorough examination of conscience structured around the seven virtues (theological and cardinal) and the seven deadly sins, helping you reflect on your internal dispositions.

categories.title: Theological Virtues
categories.description: The theological virtues (Faith, Hope, and Charity) relate directly to God and are infused by Him into the faithful.

items.text: Have I neglected to deepen my understanding of the faith through Scripture, Catechism, or spiritual reading?
items.clarification: Faith seeks understanding and grows through ongoing formation.

items.text: Have I doubted God's truths or teachings of the Church without sincerely seeking answers?
Have I been reluctant to share my faith when opportunities arose?
Have I been ashamed of my Catholic identity in certain environments or company?
Have I engaged with content (media, conversations, reading) that undermines my faith without discernment?
Have I given in to despair, believing that my sins are too great for God's mercy?
items.clarification: Hope trusts in Christ's promises and God's mercy, even when we fail.

items.text: Have I presumed on God's mercy, sinning with the expectation of easy forgiveness?
Have I placed my ultimate hope in worldly things (wealth, success, relationships) rather than in God?
Have I lost trust in God's providence during difficult times?
Have I succumbed to anxiety and worry rather than trusting God with my future?
Have I failed to love God above all things, placing other priorities before my relationship with Him?
items.clarification: Charity (love) is the greatest virtue, directing all other virtues to their proper end in God.

items.text: Have I failed to see and serve Christ in others, especially the poor, vulnerable, or difficult people?
Have I withheld forgiveness from others while seeking it for myself?
Have I been indifferent to the physical, emotional, or spiritual needs of those around me?
Have I failed to pray for others, especially those with whom I have difficulty?

categories.title: Cardinal Virtues
categories.description: The cardinal virtues (Prudence, Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance) are human virtues that can be acquired through human effort, aided by grace.

items.text: Have I made important decisions impulsively, without prayer and careful consideration?
items.clarification: Prudence is right reason in action - discerning the true good in every circumstance and choosing the right means of achieving it.

items.text: Have I sought wise counsel when needed, or insisted on my own judgment alone?
Have I failed to consider the consequences of my actions on myself and others?
Have I neglected to form my conscience properly according to Church teaching?
Have I been dishonest in my work, studies, or business dealings?
items.clarification: Justice is the constant and firm will to give God and neighbor their due.

items.text: Have I failed to make restitution for damage I've caused to others' property or reputation?
Have I given God the worship and time that is His due?
Have I treated others with the respect and dignity they deserve as children of God?
Have I been complicit in unjust systems or practices without working for change?
Have I given up in the face of difficulty rather than persevering in doing what is right?
items.clarification: Fortitude ensures firmness in difficulties and constancy in pursuing the good.

items.text: Have I chosen what is easy over what is right?
Have I avoided defending the truth out of fear of criticism or rejection?
Have I neglected to stand up for the vulnerable when I could have helped?
Have I overindulged in food, drink, entertainment, or other pleasures?
items.clarification: Temperance moderates the attraction of pleasures and provides balance in the use of created goods.

items.text: Have I used alcohol or other substances to escape my problems?
Have I allowed my devices and digital media to consume excessive time or attention?
Have I practiced moderation in all areas of my life, including work and leisure?

categories.title: Pride
categories.description: Pride is the excessive love of self and one's own excellence, placing oneself above others and even God.

items.text: Have I been unwilling to admit when I'm wrong?
items.clarification: Pride is considered the root of all sin, from which other vices grow.

items.text: Have I refused to accept criticism or correction?
Have I been boastful about my achievements or possessions?
Have I been stubborn or argumentative rather than open to others' perspectives?
Have I been overly concerned with my appearance or reputation?
Have I presumed myself to be better than others?
Have I taken credit for gifts and abilities without acknowledging God as their source?
Have I thought I could achieve holiness or solve problems through my own efforts alone, without God's grace?

categories.title: Envy
categories.description: Envy is sorrow at another's good fortune and the desire to possess what others have.

items.text: Have I resented others' success, talents, or possessions?
items.clarification: Envy sees another's good as a diminishment of oneself, rather than rejoicing in others' blessings.

items.text: Have I taken pleasure in hearing of others' failures or problems?
Have I compared myself with others in ways that lead to discontent?
Have I spoken critically of those I envy in an attempt to diminish them?
Have I failed to celebrate others' achievements and joys?
Have I allowed myself to become bitter about my own circumstances when seeing others' blessings?
Have I been competitive in unhealthy ways that harm relationships?

categories.title: Wrath (Anger)
categories.description: Wrath is uncontrolled feelings of hatred and anger that can lead to a desire for revenge.

items.text: Have I allowed anger to control my actions or words?
items.clarification: While anger itself can be justified, wrath refers to excessive or misdirected anger that harms self and others.

items.text: Have I harbored resentment or refused to forgive others?
Have I used harsh or hostile language that hurts others?
Have I wished harm or revenge on those who hurt me?
Have I been impatient or irritable with others over minor matters?
Have I allowed my anger to erupt in rage or violent behavior?
Have I been passive-aggressive rather than addressing conflicts directly and charitably?
Have I been easily triggered into anger rather than maintaining peace in difficult situations?

categories.title: Sloth (Acedia)
categories.description: Sloth is spiritual laziness that leads to neglect of spiritual growth and duties toward God and neighbor.

items.text: Have I been lukewarm in my spiritual life, doing the minimum or acting out of mere routine?
items.clarification: Sloth is not merely laziness, but a spiritual apathy that neglects love of God and neighbor.

items.text: Have I neglected prayer, sacraments, or spiritual reading due to indifference?
Have I procrastinated in doing good or fulfilling my responsibilities?
Have I wasted time in excessive entertainment, social media, or other distractions?
Have I been careless or halfhearted in my work or service to others?
Have I avoided spiritual or moral challenges that would lead to growth?
Have I neglected my duties to family, church, or community?
Have I given up on the pursuit of holiness because it seems too difficult?

categories.title: Greed (Avarice)
categories.description: Greed is the excessive desire for material possessions and wealth.

items.text: Have I been excessively concerned with acquiring money or possessions?
items.clarification: Greed distorts our relationship with material goods, turning means into ends.

items.text: Have I failed to be generous with my resources, time, and talents?
Have I been so focused on financial security that I failed to trust in God's providence?
Have I been wasteful or extravagant while neglecting to help those in need?
Have I been dishonest or unethical in financial matters?
Have I envied others' possessions or resented their prosperity?
Have I measured my worth or others' worth by material standards?
Have I failed to detach myself from material things, allowing them to become too important?

categories.title: Gluttony
categories.description: Gluttony is the overindulgence or overconsumption of food, drink, or other things to the point of waste and excess.

items.text: Have I eaten or drunk to excess, beyond what is reasonable for health and pleasure?
items.clarification: Gluttony is not just about quantity but also about an inordinate attachment to the pleasure of eating and drinking.

items.text: Have I used food or alcohol as a means of escape or comfort rather than dealing with problems?
Have I neglected moderation and discipline in my consumption habits?
Have I been wasteful with food while others go hungry?
Have I been overly concerned with food, spending excessive time or money on it?
Have I neglected fasting or abstinence as prescribed by the Church?
Have I sought instant gratification in other areas of life, unable to delay satisfaction or practice self-denial?

categories.title: Lust
categories.description: Lust is the disordered desire for sexual pleasure outside the context of marriage.

items.text: Have I deliberately entertained impure thoughts or desires?
items.clarification: Lust reduces persons to objects for pleasure rather than recognizing their inherent dignity.

items.text: Have I viewed pornography or other media that degrades the dignity of the human person?
Have I engaged in impure conversations, jokes, or entertainment?
Have I failed to guard my eyes, heart, and mind from temptations to impurity?
Have I engaged in inappropriate physical intimacy outside of marriage?
Have I treated others as objects for pleasure rather than as persons made in God's image?
Have I dressed or behaved in ways intended to tempt others to lust?
Have I neglected to cultivate the virtue of chastity according to my state in life?
